Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land-Use Patterns and Processes
Unit 7: Industrial and Economic Development Patterns and Processes

terms.def: The ability to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources.
Direction given by the compass (north, south, east, west), which does not depend on where you stand.
Distance measured in a fixed unit such as kilometers or miles.
The exact position of a place on the Earth, usually given by latitude (degrees north or south of the equator) and longitude (degrees east or west of the prime meridian).
When a group adopts some traits of another culture while keeping its own culture.
A model of African cities with three CBDs (colonial, traditional and market), ethnic neighborhoods, a mining or factory zone and informal settlements at the edge.
How a population is divided among age groups, such as children under 15, people aged 15 to 64 and people 65 and over.
The clustering of many firms in one place because being close lets them share workers, suppliers, services and ideas.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: Data made by combining values for smaller units into one value for a larger unit, such as adding provinces into a national figure. Aggregated data can hide differences between the smaller units.
A population in which older people make up a rising share, caused by low birth rates and longer lives.
The system of large companies that supply farms, run farms and process, ship and sell farm products.
The number of farmers divided by the area of arable land. A low value usually means large farms that use machines.
The raising of crops and animals on purpose for food, fiber and other products.
A boundary drawn before many settlers lived in an area, such as the US and Canada line along 49° N in the west.
A government policy that tries to lower the number of births, for example with family planning programs or limits on family size.
The farming of fish, shellfish and seaweed in ponds, tanks or ocean pens.
Land that can be used to grow crops. It leaves out deserts, ice, steep mountains and built-up areas.
The total population divided by the total land area. It shows how crowded a place is on average.
When a group takes on another culture so fully that its own traits fade away. It may be chosen or forced.
A person who has crossed a border and asked for protection as a refugee but has not yet received a decision.
A part of a state that governs many of its own affairs while the national government keeps powers such as defense. A region with fewer powers is called semiautonomous.
The breakup of a region or state into smaller states that are often hostile to each other, named for the Balkans in southeastern Europe, where Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s.
A meeting of European powers in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 that set rules for claiming land in Africa. No African rulers took part, and the borders drawn afterward often ignored African peoples.
The idea that land users bid for land with the best access to a market, so land costs more near the market and the use that can pay the most at each distance gets the land.

A practice in which real estate agents scared white owners into selling cheaply by claiming Black families were moving in, then resold the homes at higher prices; outlawed in the United States in 1968.
A suburb that has grown very fast into a large city of its own, but is not the main city of its metro area.
An invisible line, on land or at sea, that marks where the territory of one state or region ends and another begins. Also called a border.
The loss of educated, skilled people, such as doctors, nurses and engineers, when they move away from a place.
A place where goods are moved from one kind of transport to another, such as from ships to trains at a port. Processing plants often cluster there.
An abandoned or underused industrial or commercial site, such as an old factory or rail yard, whose reuse is held back by real or suspected pollution.
The number of people an area can support without damaging it. It depends on resources, technology and trade, so it is not the same as density.
A thematic map that resizes each area by a value, such as its number of people, so shapes and true sizes are given up.
An official count of all the people in a country, often taken every ten years, with facts about each household such as ages and housing.
The central business district: the commercial core of a city, with offices, stores and the highest land values.
Christaller's model of settlements as market centers serving the areas around them, with a few large, widely spaced places and many small, close ones.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: Anything that pushes the people of a place apart and divides them, such as two languages in separate regions or a deep religious divide.
Anything that pulls the people of a place together and unites them, such as a shared language, a national holiday or a shared religion.
Migration in which people follow relatives or neighbors who moved before them, often to the same place.
A narrow passage on a major route, such as a strait or canal, that many ships must use, so whoever controls it holds power over the traffic. Examples: the Suez Canal, the Strait of Hormuz.
A thematic map that shades whole areas, such as countries or provinces, by classes of a measure. It works best for rates and percents.
A large, dense settlement where most people earn a living from work other than farming, such as trade, government and services.
terms.topicTitle: The Origin and Influences of Urbanization

terms.def: A rural settlement pattern in which homes are grouped together in a village, with farmland around it; also called nucleated settlement.
A pattern in which things are grouped close together in one or a few places.
A group of people born in the same years, such as everyone aged 20 to 24. Each bar of a population pyramid is a cohort.
One country taking control of another place and its people, governing them directly and often sending settlers there.
The transfer of plants, animals, diseases and people between the Americas and Africa, Europe and Asia that began after Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492.
Farming mainly to sell crops and animals for profit, as on soybean farms in Mato Grosso, Brazil.
The series of steps that turns a farm product into something a consumer buys: inputs, growing, processing, distribution and sale.
Relying on one or a few raw exports, such as coffee or cocoa, for most of a country's export earnings, which makes its income rise and fall with world prices.
An arrangement in which members pay a local farm in advance for a share of its harvest and share its risk; also called CSA.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country: giving up less of other goods to make it. Trade follows comparative advantage.
When one place has a supply of something that another place needs, so trade between them makes sense.
Burgess's 1925 model, based on Chicago, in which a city grows outward in rings around the CBD, from a zone in transition to a commuter zone.
A boundary drawn to follow a cultural line, such as language or religion. Also called an ethnographic boundary. Example: India and Pakistan (1947).
Expansion diffusion from person to person and from place to nearby place, like a ripple, regardless of size or power.
The sea from 12 to 24 nautical miles from a state's coast, where the state may enforce its customs, immigration, tax and health laws.
In world-system terms, the countries with mostly high-wage service, research and decision jobs and advanced industry. A model category, not an official list.
The mixing of different cultures in one place into a new local form, such as a new language, food or music.
The number of births in a year for every 1,000 people in a population.
The number of deaths in a year for every 1,000 people in a population.
Places and cultures growing more alike as they share the same products, media, styles and languages.
Places and cultures growing or staying different, often because a group protects or revives its own language and customs.
The land as people have changed it: buildings, fields, roads, signs and places of worship laid over the physical landscape.
Trying to understand a practice by the standards of the culture it belongs to, before judging it.
The shared practices, beliefs, objects and behaviors that a group of people learns and passes on to the next generation.
One single part of a culture, such as a food, a greeting, a style of house, a holiday or a way of using land.
The clearing of forest, often for farms, pasture or wood, as in parts of the Amazon basin of Brazil.
The decline of factory jobs and industry in a region, as factories close, move away or replace workers with machines.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: Marking a boundary on the ground with posts, fences, walls or buoys. Before that, a boundary is defined (described in a treaty) and delimited (drawn on maps); after it, it is administered (run day to day).
A strip of land along a boundary where armed forces are not allowed, set up by agreement, such as the zone between North Korea and South Korea since 1953 (the DMZ).
The spread of democratic government, in which people choose their leaders in free elections, to places that did not have it.
A model of how birth and death rates change over time in five stages: deaths fall first, then births, so population growth speeds up and then slows or turns negative.
The number of people under 15 and 65 and over for every 100 people aged 15 to 64. The youth and elderly ratios count each group alone.
A theory that says poorer countries stay poor because of their dependence on richer ones, built through colonial rule and trade in raw materials for factory goods.
The degrading of dry land until it can support far fewer plants, animals and people, linked to drought, overgrazing and clearing, as in parts of the Sahel.
The process of improving the material conditions of people's lives, such as income, health, education and choices.
The transfer of power from a national government to regional governments. It can range from more regional self-rule to a region breaking away as a new state.
A regional version of one language, with its own words, pronunciation or grammar, that speakers of other versions can still mostly understand.
The spread of a culture trait, idea or invention from one place to other places over time.
One of the poorest, least-served parts of a city, such as an area of abandoned buildings or of unsafe land where the newest arrivals settle.
A pattern in which things are spread out over an area rather than grouped together.
A rural settlement pattern in which homes are spread out, usually one farmhouse on each farm, as in the US Midwest.
The idea that contact between places falls as the distance between them grows.
A change in shape, area, distance or direction that happens when the round Earth is drawn on a flat map.
The slow change of wild plants and animals into crops and livestock, as people chose which ones to plant or breed over many generations.
A thematic map that shows counts as dots, each standing for a set number, such as 10,000 people.
The number of years a population takes to double at a steady growth rate. By the rule of 70, it is about 70 divided by the growth rate in percent.
The area of productive land and water needed to supply what a population uses and to absorb its waste, usually far larger than the area the population lives on.
The lower cost of each unit produced that comes from producing more, because fixed costs such as machines are spread over more output.
Tourism to natural areas that aims to protect the environment and benefit local people, for example by hiring local guides and limiting visitors.
The parts of Earth’s surface where people live permanently. Very cold, dry or high places lie mostly outside it.
A suburban center of offices, malls and hotels, usually near highway junctions, with more jobs than residents.
The height of the land above sea level, often shown on maps with lines of equal height or with colors.
An old, rejected idea that the physical environment, especially climate, decides how people live and behave. It was used to justify European rule over other peoples.
The unequal burden of pollution and environmental harm on poor and minority communities.
A model of how the main causes of death change as a society changes: from infections and famine to chronic diseases such as heart disease and cancer, with new infections possible.
The forced removal of an ethnic group from an area, by killing, terror or expulsion, so that another group controls it. A UN court found it took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 1990s.
An area within a city or town where many people of one ethnic group live, often marked by their language on signs, their shops and their places of worship.
A religion tied to one people and their homeland, which mostly stays near its hearth or spreads when followers migrate. AP® Human Geography classes Hinduism and Judaism this way.
A movement by an ethnic group inside a state to win independence or self-rule for the region where it lives, such as in Quebec or Catalonia.
Identity with a group of people who share ancestry, history and cultural traditions. It is cultural, not biological.
Judging another culture by the standards of your own culture, often seeing your own as the right or best way.
A strong sense of belonging to one's ethnic nation, often with the wish that the nation govern itself. It can unite a nation-state or, for a minority, pull toward separation.
terms.topicTitle: Consequences of Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces

terms.def: An exclusive economic zone: the sea up to 200 nautical miles from a state's coast, where that state has the rights to fish, oil, gas and other resources.
Spread of a trait outward from its hearth while it stays strong where it began. It has three kinds: contagious, hierarchical and stimulus.
Farming that uses few inputs on each unit of land, spread over large areas, as in ranching on the Pampas of Argentina.
A rural-looking area beyond the suburbs, with homes on large lots, whose residents mostly commute into the metro area.

A state whose government has lost control of much of its territory and cannot provide basic services such as security, courts or clean water. Somalia after its government collapsed in 1991 is a common example.
terms.topicTitle: Consequences of Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces

terms.def: A labeling system in which buyers pay producers, often in less developed countries, a minimum price and a premium, under set labor and environmental rules.
A state in which a constitution divides power between a national government and regional governments (states or provinces), each with its own powers. Example: Germany, the United States.
The schooling that girls and women receive. More of it is linked to later marriage, fewer children and fewer child deaths.
An arc of land in Southwest Asia, from the eastern Mediterranean along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, where wheat, barley, sheep and goats were among the first species domesticated.
Collecting data by going to a place to watch, count, sketch, photograph or interview people there.
The shift from hunting and gathering to farming that began about 12,000 to 10,000 years ago in several hearths; also called the Neolithic Revolution.
A movement of people, goods, money or ideas from one place to another.
Culture kept by a small, close group, often rural, taught by family and community, and slow to change. Plain dress and barn raisings among the Amish are examples.
An area where people have poor access to affordable, healthy food, often a low-income area far from any supermarket.
Not having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food.
Migration in which people are made to move, by enslavement, war, persecution or disaster, and have no real choice to stay.
A region whose places share one or more measurable traits, such as a main language, a climate or a main crop. Also called a uniform region.
A region tied together by flows to and from a center, such as the area a city's commuters come from or a newspaper delivers to. Also called a nodal region.
A model of car-based US metro areas in which an old downtown is ringed by suburbs and edge cities spaced along a beltway; also called the peripheral model.
Gender Inequality Index: a UNDP measure of gaps between women and men in reproductive health, empowerment and the labor market. Lower means less inequality.
The difference between what women and men earn on average, often shown as women's pay as a percent of men's.

A genetically modified organism: a plant or animal whose genes were changed in a lab, for example by adding a gene from another species. The first GMO food went on sale in 1994, and GMO crops spread widely on farms from the late 1990s.
The movement of higher-income residents and investment into a lower-income neighborhood, raising property values and often displacing long-time renters.
Information tied to a location, such as where something is or how much of it is found in a place.
A geographic information system: computer software that stores data tied to locations as layers, so they can be mapped and compared on one map.
A boundary drawn as a straight line, often along a line of latitude or longitude, such as 49° N between the United States and Canada.
Drawing voting district boundaries to give one party or group an advantage. Packing crowds the other side's voters into a few districts; cracking splits them across many.
The scale of analysis that looks at the whole world, comparing places across it.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: The network of steps, places and companies that a product passes through from farm to consumer, often across several countries.
The growing connection of places around the world through trade, travel, media and the internet, so goods, money, people and ideas move faster and farther.
A thematic map that uses symbols, usually circles, sized by the amount at each place.
A model that predicts interaction between two places grows with their populations and falls with the square of the distance between them.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: The spread of high-yield seeds, chemical fertilizer, irrigation, pesticides and machines to farms in many less developed countries, from about the 1960s to the 1980s; sometimes called the Third Agricultural Revolution.
A ring of protected farmland, parks and forest around a city where building is restricted; an urban growth boundary is a line beyond which building is limited.
Gross domestic product: the value of all goods and services produced inside a country's borders in a year, whoever owns the firms.
Gross national income: all income earned by a country's residents, at home and abroad. GNI per capita divides it by the population.
Gross national product: the value of goods and services produced by a country's people and firms, wherever in the world they produce it.
A key industry or major investment, often planned, whose growth spreads to the region around it through the multiplier effect.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: A person allowed into another country to work for a set time, who is expected to return home.
The place where a culture trait, idea or invention began, and from which it spread.
Expansion diffusion from larger or more powerful places or people to smaller or less powerful ones, skipping places in between. Reverse hierarchical diffusion runs from small places up to large ones.
A crop variety bred, by crossing plants, to produce much more grain per hectare when given water and fertilizer, such as the wheat bred in Mexico and the rice IR8.
Human Development Index: a UNDP measure from 0 to 1 that combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita).
A government’s rules about who may move into the country, how many people and for how long.
A country extending its power and influence over other places by force, money or culture, whether or not it rules them directly.
A zoning policy that requires or rewards developers for including homes priced for lower- and middle-income households in new buildings.
An organized effort by a people under foreign or outside rule to win a state of their own, such as India's movement that ended British rule in 1947.
The spread of factories, machines and new sources of power to a place, so that goods are made in factories rather than by hand. It began in Great Britain in the late 1700s.
The number of babies who die before their first birthday for every 1,000 live births.
Building new homes or businesses on vacant or underused lots inside an area that is already built up, instead of on open land at the edge.
Work that is not registered, taxed or counted by the government, such as street selling or day labor paid in cash.
The basic physical systems and public facilities a place needs to function, such as roads, rail, water and sewer pipes, power grids, communication networks, schools and clinics.
terms.topicTitle: Consequences of Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces

terms.def: Farming that puts many inputs (labor, money, machines, fertilizer, water) into each unit of land to get a large output from it, as in market gardening near Rotterdam.
Migration within one country. Interregional migration goes between regions; intraregional migration stays within one region.
A person forced to leave home who stays inside his or her own country.
The split of the stages of making a product among different countries, by their skills and costs.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: The International Monetary Fund: a body set up in 1944 that lends to governments in financial trouble, often on conditions such as spending cuts and open markets (structural adjustment).
The sea beyond any state's exclusive economic zone, more than 200 nautical miles from the coast, open to ships of all states. Also called the high seas.
Something between the origin and the destination that makes a move harder, such as distance, cost, a border, a sea or rough land.
An attraction along the way, such as a job offer, that may lead a migrant to stop before reaching the planned destination.
A state's claim to territory in another state where people of its own nation live, such as Germany's 1938 claim to the Sudetenland in Czechoslovakia.
Supplying water to crops by canals, pipes, ditches or sprinklers, so land can be farmed where rain alone is not enough.
A thematic map with lines that join points of equal value, such as the same height or the same temperature.
Delivering parts to a factory just when they are needed, so little stock is kept.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: How people use an area of land, such as for forest, farms, homes, roads or factories.
A group of languages that grew from one ancient ancestor language. Indo-European, which includes English, Spanish and Hindi, is one.
A model of Latin American cities with a CBD by the main plaza, a wealthy commercial spine, rings that get poorer outward and squatter settlements at the edge.
A model that says a factory locates where its total costs of transport, labor and nearby firms are lowest. Weight-losing industries locate near raw materials, weight-gaining ones near markets.
The box on a map that says what each color, shade, symbol or line stands for, often with the units. Also called a key.
The average number of years a newborn can expect to live if the death rates of its birth year stay the same.
Something a data source cannot show or may get wrong, such as being out of date, missing some people or giving one value for a large area.
A rural settlement pattern in which homes line up along a road, river, canal or coast, as along the Nile in Egypt.
A language that people with different home languages use to communicate with each other, often for trade or work.
The share of adults in a population who can read and write.
The scale of analysis that looks at a part of a country, such as a province, state, city or neighborhood. Data for parts of a country are also called subnational.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: A survey method that divides land into long, narrow strips running back from a river, so each owner has river frontage; used by French settlers in Quebec and Louisiana.
Thomas Malthus’s idea (1798) that population grows faster than the food supply, so famine, disease or war will follow unless people have fewer children.
A drawing of part or all of the Earth's surface that shows where things are or how something varies from place to place. Every map selects what to show and leaves the rest out.
A method for flattening the round Earth onto a flat map. Every projection distorts shape, area, distance or direction in some way.
The ratio between a distance on a map and the same distance on the ground, such as 1:50,000. A large-scale map shows a small area in detail; a small-scale map shows a large area with less detail.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: Intensive growing of fruits, vegetables and flowers for nearby city markets; also called truck farming.
Replacing human and animal labor with machines, such as reapers and tractors.
Farming suited to hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters, growing crops such as olives, grapes and citrus in places like southern Spain and central Chile.
An urban area with 10 million people or more. The threshold is a convention, and a city's count depends on where its edge is drawn.
An urban area with 20 million people or more, a convention UN-Habitat used for the largest megacities.
A survey method that marks land by distances and by natural or human features such as streams, trees and walls, giving irregular parcels; used in the eastern United States.
Making very small loans, often to women in groups, to people too poor to borrow from ordinary banks, usually to start or grow a small business. Also called microcredit or microloans.
A long-term move from one place to another to live, within a country or across a border.
Intensive farming that raises crops and animals on the same farm, often feeding the crops to the animals, as in the US Corn Belt.
Development that puts homes, shops and offices in the same building or block, such as apartments above stores.
Growing the same crop on the same field year after year. Monoculture, a close term, means growing one crop over a large area.
Many cultures living side by side in one society, each keeping its own traits; also a policy that supports this.
A state that holds two or more nations, such as Nigeria or Belgium.
Harris and Ullman's 1945 model in which a city has several centers, such as a CBD, a port, a university and an industrial district, each drawing its own land uses.
The way new jobs in one industry create more jobs in others, as workers spend wages and suppliers grow; it also works in reverse when a plant closes.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: A nation whose people live in two or more states, such as Koreans in North Korea and South Korea.
A group of people who share a culture, such as a language, history or religion, and see themselves as one people, often with a homeland.
A state whose people are mostly one nation, so the nation and the state cover about the same area. Iceland is often given as an example.
The scale of analysis that looks at one country as a whole, with one value for each country.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: Something from nature that people use, such as water, soil, fish, forests, oil or sunlight. Renewable resources replace themselves; nonrenewable resources are used up.
A later thinker who shares Malthus’s worry and extends it to water, energy and the environment, arguing that population growth should slow.
The use of economic or political pressure, such as loans, trade or control of a currency, by powerful states or companies to influence former colonies without ruling them directly.
Policies that shrink the government's role in the economy: freer trade, lower tariffs, selling state-owned firms and cutting government spending.
A design movement that builds neighborhoods like older towns, with walkable street grids, homes near the sidewalk, a town center and a mix of housing.
A country whose economy has shifted quickly from farming toward factories and exports, such as South Korea from the 1960s.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: Extensive agriculture in which people move herds of animals to fresh grass and water with the seasons, as in Mongolia; also called pastoral nomadism.
Hiring another firm to do part of a company's work, often in another country where costs are lower (offshoring).
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: How things are arranged across space, such as clustered, dispersed or in a line along a river.
A region defined by what people believe or feel about places, such as "the South" in the United States. Also called a vernacular region.
In world-system terms, countries where many people do primary-sector and low-wage work, often exporting raw materials. A model category, not an official list.
The total population divided by the area of arable land. It shows how many people each unit of farmland must feed.
A simple mixed language that grows when groups with no shared language must trade or work together. No one speaks it as a first language; if children do, it becomes a creole.
A location plus the meaning, character and feelings people give it. Those feelings are called a sense of place.
People shaping a place, with murals, festivals, signs or buildings, to express who they are and build a shared sense of place.
Intensive farming of one crop, such as oil palm, bananas or tea, on a large estate, usually in the tropics, for sale far away.
Culture shared by large, mixed groups of people in many places, spread by media and business, and quick to change, such as hit songs, chain restaurants and fashion.
All the people who live in a place, such as a city, a country or the whole world.
The number of people for each unit of land, usually per square kilometer.
The pattern of where people live across an area: where they are clustered and where there are few.
A bar graph that shows a population by age and sex: males on the left, females on the right, youngest at the bottom.
The idea that the physical environment sets limits and offers options, and people choose how to live within them using their culture and technology.

Flexible production in smaller batches, spread among many firms and places, with just-in-time delivery; it followed Fordism, the mass production of identical goods on assembly lines in one large plant.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: A building style from about the 1970s on that mixes older and newer styles on purpose, often with playful shapes; it looks similar in cities around the world.
The part of the economy that takes resources straight from nature: farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
A country's largest city when it is far larger than the second city (often more than twice as large) and dominates the country's economy, government and culture.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: A government policy that tries to raise the number of births, for example with payments for each child, paid parental leave or cheaper child care.
An attraction at the place a migrant goes that draws people in, such as jobs, safety or relatives already there.
A problem at the place a migrant leaves that drives people away, such as low pay, drought or war.
Data in the form of words, pictures and experiences, such as interviews, field notes, photos and travel accounts.
Data that are numbers you can count or measure, such as the number of stalls on a street or the yearly rainfall of a city.
The part of the service economy that creates and moves information, such as research, software and finance.
The part of the service economy where the highest-level decisions are made, by top officers of big firms and governments.
Extensive raising of cattle or sheep that graze large areas of fixed land, usually for sale to distant buyers.
In central place theory, the greatest distance people will travel to buy a good or service.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: A model in which the city of rank n in a country has about 1/n the population of the largest city, giving a smooth ladder of city sizes.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: The crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, given as a percent (divide by 10). It leaves out migration.

Patterns of migration that E. G. Ravenstein drew from British census data in 1885 and 1889: most moves are short, many happen in steps, long-distance migrants go to large cities, each flow has a counterflow, and within a country women moved more than men.

Redrawing the boundaries of voting districts so that each holds about the same number of people, in the United States after each census. Reapportionment, a different step, shares out seats among states first.
Refusing loans, insurance or other services, or offering worse terms, based on a property's location; in US history it was aimed mostly at Black and immigrant neighborhoods.
A map that shows where things are, such as borders, cities, roads and rivers, with no single theme.
A person who has crossed an international border to escape danger or persecution and has been recognized as needing protection.
An area that geographers group together because its places share something: a trait, a tie to a center or a shared belief.
The scale of analysis that looks at a part of the world made of several countries, such as South Asia or Latin America.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: Direction that depends on the speaker's point of view, such as "up north" or "the Far East".
How far a place feels, measured in time, cost or ease of travel instead of kilometers.
Where a place is compared with other places or features, such as "near the center of the United States, where two rivers meet".
A boundary that no longer works as a border but can still be seen in the cultural landscape, such as the old line between East and West Germany.
Spread of a trait when people who hold it move to a new place and take it with them.
Money that a migrant sends back to family or community in the place of origin.
Gathering data about the Earth from a distance, usually with satellites or aircraft that record images or light.
The total fertility rate at which each generation just replaces itself: about 2.1 births per woman where few children die.
The number of housing units or people on a given area of land; apartments give high density, detached houses on large lots give low density.
A model by W. W. Rostow (1960) that says countries develop through five stages: traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity and high mass consumption.
The scoring guide readers use to mark an answer. On the AP® Human Geography exam each part has one point and one rubric line saying what earns it.
terms.topicTitle: How FRQs Are Scored and What Each Task Verb Demands

terms.def: Migration from the countryside to cities.
The buildup of salt in soil, often after years of irrigation in hot, dry places where water evaporates and leaves its salts behind.
A satellite navigation system, such as the United States' GPS, that uses signals from satellites to find the exact location of a receiver like a phone.
The size of the unit that data describe or that a question is about: global, regional, national or local. It is set by the data, not by the size of the map.
terms.topicTitle: Scale of Analysis and Map Scale

terms.def: A period of new farming methods and machines (crop rotation, selective breeding, enclosure, the seed drill and reaper) that began in Britain in the 1700s and spread to North America in the 1800s, raising output per worker.
The part of the economy that turns raw materials into goods, such as factories and building.
Hoyt's 1939 model in which land uses form wedges that spread outward from the CBD along transport lines, with high-rent wedges continuing in one direction.
The right of a people (a nation) to choose its own political status, such as independence or self-rule inside a larger state.
In world-system terms, countries between the core and the periphery, with a large factory sector and growing services. A model category, not an official list.
The idea that each group that lives in a place leaves marks on the landscape that later groups keep, change or reuse, so the landscape has layers.
The number of males for every 100 females in a population or an age group.
A region caught between stronger outside powers, often divided inside by culture or politics, where conflict is common. Eastern Europe during the Cold War is a common example.
Extensive farming in which people clear and burn a forest plot, farm it for a few years and then move on while the old plot rests and regrows; also called slash and burn or swidden.
The physical character of a place itself, such as its landforms, water, soil and climate.
The location of a place relative to other places, routes and features, which shapes its links to them.
Planning policies that steer new building into compact, walkable, connected areas near existing services and transit instead of spreading onto farmland.
A line under a map, table or chart that says who made the data and in what year, or that the data are invented for practice.
A model of Southeast Asian cities centered on the old colonial port, with commercial, government and mixed zones, new suburbs and market gardens at the edge.
A state's right and power to govern its own territory and people without control from outside.
The area between and around places, and how people and things are arranged across it.

An area with lower taxes, fewer rules and cheaper land for firms making goods for export, such as Shenzhen, China. Free-trade zones, export-processing zones and Mexico's maquiladoras are related forms.
terms.topicTitle: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

terms.def: Housing built by residents on land they do not legally own or rent, often lacking piped water, sewers and secure title; also called an informal settlement.
A country: an area with a permanent population, a defined territory and a government that controls it, recognized by other states. The UN has 193 member states.
A nation that has no independent state of its own, such as the Kurds of Southwest Asia.
Migration made in stages, such as from a village to a town and then to a large city.
Expansion diffusion in which an idea spreads but people change it to fit their own culture, so the trait takes a new form.
A boundary drawn after an area was settled, as the cultural landscape took shape, such as the boundary between China and Viet Nam.
Farming mainly to feed the farmer's own family, with little left to sell, as on small rice plots in rural Bangladesh.
The movement of people, jobs and stores from a central city to the lower-density suburbs around it.
A boundary forced on an area by an outside power, often without regard for the peoples who live there, such as many borders in Africa drawn by European empires.

Cooperation among three or more states through an organization for shared goals, such as defense, trade or protecting the environment, in which members give up some sovereignty. Examples: the EU, NATO, the African Union.
Information gathered by asking a sample of people the same set of questions, such as the American Community Survey; results are estimates with a margin of error.
Using land and resources so that people now meet their needs without harming the ability of future people to meet theirs.
Development that improves people's lives now without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing the economy, society and the environment.
The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals adopted by all UN member states in 2015, to be reached by 2030, such as no poverty, gender equality and climate action.
The blending of traits from two or more cultures into a new form, such as a festival or religion that neither culture had before.
A tax on imported goods. It raises their price, which protects a country's own producers.
The word in a question that says what your answer must do, such as identify, describe, explain or compare.
terms.topicTitle: How FRQs Are Scored and What Each Task Verb Demands

terms.def: Cutting a hillside into flat steps so it can be farmed and so soil and water stay in place, as on the Ifugao rice terraces of the Philippines.
The sea up to 12 nautical miles from a state's coast, which the state rules much as it rules its land, though foreign ships may pass through peacefully.
The attempt by a person, group or state to influence or control people and things by claiming control over an area, such as with fences, signs, flags or border guards.
The use of violence, especially against civilians, to create fear and reach a political goal.
The part of the economy that provides services, such as shops, transport, health care and teaching. Also called the service sector.
A map that shows one topic or measure across places, such as income, rainfall or the number of people, with a legend that explains it.
In central place theory, the fewest customers a seller needs to stay in business.
terms.topicTitle: The Size and Distribution of Cities

terms.def: The way faster transport and communication cut the time needed to link places, so distant places feel closer.
A place name. Toponyms often record who named or settled a place, such as the Spanish names of Santa Fe and Los Angeles.
The average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime if the birth rates of one year stayed the same.
A survey method that divides land into a grid of townships 6 miles square, each with 36 sections of 1 square mile; set up by the US Land Ordinance of 1785.
A group of countries that lower or remove tariffs and other trade barriers among themselves, such as the European Union or Mercosur.
Buildings made in a long-standing local style, usually with local materials, such as adobe homes in New Mexico or thatched cottages in Ireland.
The seasonal movement of herders and their animals between pastures, such as to mountains in summer and valleys in winter.
Dense, mixed-use building within a short walk of a rail or rapid bus station, so people can live and work without a car.
The area at the edge of a region where its defining trait fades and another region begins, such as the Sahel between the Sahara and the grasslands to the south.
Migration in which people keep strong ties to both their country of origin and their new country.
A change in data over time, described by its direction (rising or falling), its dates and how much it changed.
A state in which the national government holds most power; regions carry out national decisions and have only the powers the national government gives them. Example: France.

terms.term: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
terms.def: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), adopted in 1982: the treaty that sets the sea zones each coastal state may claim.
A religion that seeks followers from any place or group and spreads widely. AP® Human Geography classes Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and Sikhism this way.
A ranking of cities by the size of the area they serve and control, from a few world cities at the top to many small towns at the base.
A government program that buys, clears and rebuilds areas judged to be run-down, often displacing the people who lived there.
The spread of a city at low density over a large area, often across farmland, with homes, shops and jobs far apart.
The process by which a growing share of a population lives in cities, through migration to cities and their growth.
terms.topicTitle: The Origin and Influences of Urbanization

terms.def: A farm product processed, branded or certified to earn more per unit, such as farmstead cheese or organic produce.
Migration in which people choose to move, usually for work, family, study or a better life.
A model of rural land use, published by Johann Heinrich von Thünen in 1826, in which transport cost to one market sets land use in rings: market gardening and dairy, forest, grain, then ranching.
How easy and safe it is to reach daily needs, such as shops, school and work, on foot.
The work women do in growing, processing, distributing and preparing food, which varies by place, culture, laws and the type of farming.
A city whose companies, banks and organizations make decisions that reach across the world economy; also called a global city. Its rank comes from its functions and links, not its population.
Immanuel Wallerstein's model of one connected world economy in which countries play core, semiperiphery or periphery roles, and can move between them.
Local laws that divide a city into zones and set what may be built in each, such as homes, stores or factories, and how tall or dense.
